extracted.intended_audience: poets, spoken-word performers, slam organizers, and general readers interested in poetry slams
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for organizing, performing in, and judging poetry slam competitions, including format, scoring, prohibitions, and stylistic/performative considerations. Covers common practices (judge selection, time limits, scoring scale) and variations (theme slams, open/invitational formats).

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance and content judged
rubrics_metrics.description: The performances at a poetry slam are judged as much on performance as content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judging typically accounts for both the spoken delivery and the written/lyrical content; performers are evaluated on stage presence, vocal delivery, and textual quality. Different slams may weight performance vs. content differently; the page notes that performance is as important as content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring scale (0–10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores generally range between zero and ten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After each poet performs, a score is awarded to the performance using this numeric scale. Scores from different judges are aggregated to determine standings across rounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge selection and panel size
rubrics_metrics.description: The judging is often handled by a panel of judges, typically five, who are usually selected from the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels are commonly composed of audience members chosen by the MC; the typical panel size is five but may vary. Selection method and panel size affect scoring variability and should be made explicit in event rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a 'sacrificial' poet to calibrate judges
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the competition begins, the host will often bring up a 'sacrificial' poet, whom the judges will score in order to calibrate their judging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A warm-up/calibration performance helps judges align scoring expectations; this is a common practice to reduce score inflation/deflation across judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit enforcement and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Other rules for slams include enforcing a time limit, after which a poet's score may be docked based on how long the poem exceeded the limit for. The time limit is usually around three to four minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizers should set and announce a time limit (commonly 3–4 minutes) and define the penalty/docking policy for overtime. Some slams vary time limits (e.g., 1-2-3 format) especially in theme or specialty slams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of props, costumes, and music
rubrics_metrics.description: Props, costumes, and music are typically forbidden in slams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prohibition distinguishes traditional slam from broader performance poetry; exceptions may be allowed in theme slams or special formats (e.g., Swedish 'Triathlon' slams that permit a musician and dancer). Event rules should state whether such elements are allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition format and elimination structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A single round at a standard slam consists of performances by all eligible poets. Most slams last multiple rounds, and many involve the elimination of lower-scoring poets in successive rounds. An elimination format might run 8–4–2; eight poets in the first round, four in the second, and two in the last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizers should define the number of rounds, elimination thresholds, and how points carry between rounds. The winner is the poet with the highest number of points earned across rounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open versus Invitational formats
rubrics_metrics.description: In an 'Open Slam', the most common slam type, competition is open to all who wish to compete, given the number of slots available. In an 'Invitational Slam', only those invited to do so may compete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide and publicize whether the event is open-entry or by invitation; this affects accessibility, diversity of competitors, and logistical planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme slams and formal constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Theme Slam' is one in which all performances must conform to a specified theme, genre, or formal constraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theme slams may change other rules (e.g., allow costumes, change judging structure, alter time limits) and are often used to encourage participation from particular or underrepresented demographics. Examples include Nerd, Erotica, Queer, Improv, 'Dead Poet Slam' (work by deceased poets), and '1-2-3' time formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master of ceremonies (MC) role
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the audience are chosen by a master of ceremonies (MC) to act as judges for the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MC typically manages judge selection, announces rules and time limits, brings up sacrificial poets, and guides event flow. The MC's conduct can shape fairness and the tone of judging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience response as a scoring input
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the poets are judged by audience response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some slams use crowd reaction as an explicit scoring mechanism (or an informal indicator); reliance on audience response can skew results toward more immediately entertaining or populist performances and may disadvantage subtler work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performative style diversity and delivery techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry slams can feature a broad range of voices, styles, cultural traditions, and approaches to writing and performance (e.g., hip-hop-influenced delivery, dub poetry, unrhyming narrative, shifting voices/tones, ironic monotone, tap-dancing, beatboxing, choreography).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful styles change over time; slams often encourage experimentation with vocal delivery and physical performance. Organizers and judges should be aware of cultural traditions (e.g., dub poetry) and avoid biased preference for a single 'slam voice'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic depth and stylistic range (criticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slam poetry has been criticized for lacking depth and for its features, e.g., 'slam voice,' which may limit the range of emotion it can express.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argue that competitive framing and stylistic homogeneity can produce performative clichés and emotional manipulation. Event organizers and judges can use this critique to promote stylistic diversity and reward substantive, varied work rather than formulaic performance.
